'''''Prunus salicina''''' ([[Synonym (taxonomy)|syn.]] ''Prunus triflora'' or ''Prunus thibetica''), commonly called the '''Chinese plum''' or '''Japanese plum''',<ref name=EPPO>{{cite web | title = ''Prunus salicina'' | url = https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/PRNSC | publisher = [[European and Mediterranean Plant Protection Organization]] (EPPO) | access-date = 10 January 2023}}</ref> is a small, [[deciduous]] tree native to China, Taiwan, and Southeast Asia. It is an introduced species in Korea, Japan, the United States, and Australia.

''Prunus salicina'' should not be confused with ''[[Prunus mume]]'', a related species also commonly called Chinese plum; or the [[loquat]], which is also known as the Japanese or Chinese Plum. ''[[Prunus japonica]]'' is another tree that is a separate species despite having a Latin name similar to ''Prunus salicina'''s common name.

== Names ==
Some names for this plant, in addition to Japanese or Chinese plum, are willow-leaf cherry, Asian plum, in English, ''ameixa'' or ''ameixa-japonesa'' in Portuguese, 李 lǐ in Mandarin, and ''Japanskt plommon'' in Swedish.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |title=Prunus salicina Lindl. |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/3021120 |access-date=2023-01-28 |website=www.gbif.org |language=en}}</ref>

The Latin [[genus|generic]] name ''[[wikt:prunus#Latin|Prunus]]'' derives from the Ancient Greek [[wikt:προύνη|προύνη]] (''proúnē''), meaning plum.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Prunus - FNA |url=http://floranorthamerica.org/Prunus |access-date=2023-01-28 |website=floranorthamerica.org}}</ref> The specific epithet, ''salicina'', is derived from the Latin word for [[willow]], since the leaves of ''Prunus salicina'' have a narrow, lanceolate, and taper-pointed shape, which is similar to the leaves of some willow species.

==Description==
''Prunus salicina'' grows up to {{convert|9-12|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall, and its branches are purplish- to reddish-brown, and its lateral shoots are yellowish-red.{{citation needed|date=December 2023}}

The leaves are 6–12 cm long and 2.5–5 cm broad, with scalloped margins, which when young are often mixed with simple, gland-tipped teeth. The leaves' shapes tend to be oblong, though they sometimes vary to slightly more obovate (broader above the middle), narrowly elliptic, or in rare cases slightly ovate (broader half below the middle). The base of the leaf is wedge-shaped, and its apex ranges from acute (pointed) to caudate (having a slender, short tail). The upper side of the leaf is dark green and lustrous, and has six or seven secondary veins on either side of midvein, not extending to the leaf margin.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Prunus salicina in Flora of China @ efloras.org |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200011159 |access-date=2023-01-24 |website=www.efloras.org}}</ref>

The winter buds of ''P. salicina'' are purplish red and are rarely hairy at scale [[Margin (botany)|margins]]. The flowers are produced in early spring, around April, each about 2 cm in diameter with five white petals, and they grow in groups of three. The [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicel]] is 1.0–1.5 cm, and its [[sepal]]s are oblong-ovate and about 5 mm, hairless on the outside, with loosely serrated margins. The sepal's apex is acute to obtuse. The petals of the flower are white and oblong-obovate, with a wedge-shaped base and a jagged margin near the apex. The [[Ovary (botany)|ovary]] is hairless and the [[Stigma (botany)|stigma]] is disc-shaped.<ref name=":0" />

The fruit is a [[drupe]], 4–7 cm in diameter, with yellow-pink flesh,  The skin can be yellow, red, or sometimes green or purple, and has a powdery coating. The shape of the drupe is spherical, egg-shaped, or conical, and it is 3.5–5 cm in diameter, though it can reach 7 cm in diameter in horticultural forms.<ref name=":0" /> The trees fruit from July to August. When fully ripe, fruit can be eaten raw.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://homeorchard.ucanr.edu/Fruits_&_Nuts/Plum_and_Prune|title=Plum and Prune (Japanese: Prunus salicina; European: Prunus domestica)}}</ref> In comparison to ''P. domestica,'' ''P. salicina'', fruit has a higher flavor and aroma, better texture, more color, bigger size, and good nutritional values.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last1=Barzamini Reza Fotouhi Ghazvini |first1=Sadegh |last2=Ghazvini |first2=Reza Fotouhi |date=11 July 2017 |title=Pollinizer Influence on Fruit Quality Traits in Japanese Plum (Prunus salicina Lindl.) |url=https://ijhst.ut.ac.ir/article_66759_d1eba9adb0f07b95b65e0d75260c75db.pdf |access-date=24 January 2023 |website=International Journal of Horticultural Science and Technology}}</ref>

The pit of ''P. salicina'' is ovoid to oblong and wrinkled.<ref name=":0" />

=== Growth pattern ===
The Japanese plum, like other ''Prunus'' species, is mostly self-incompatible, so requires cross pollination to ensure fruit set because this genus is unable to bear fruit parthenocarpically. Several cultivars or varieties, however, have been found to be  self-compatibile.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Guerra |first1=M.E. |last2=Rodrigo |first2=J. |date=2015 |title=Japanese plum pollination: A review |journal=Scientia Horticulturae |volume=197 |pages=674–686 |doi=10.1016/j.scienta.2015.10.032 |issn=0304-4238}}</ref>

== Distribution and habitat==
''P. salicina'' is native to China, Taiwan, Myanmar, Laos, and Vietnam.<ref name="iucn status 18 November 2021"/> In China, it grows in sparse forests, forest margins, thickets, along trails in mountains, and stream sides in valleys, at elevations of 200–2600 m.<ref name=":0" /> It grows best in temperate warmer regions, as it requires moderate temperatures and is usually early flowering.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Torrecillas |first1=Arturo |chapter=Chapter 5 - Agronomical Effects of Deficit Irrigation in Apricot, Peach, and Plum Trees |date=2018-01-01 |chapter-url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780128131640000053 |title=Water Scarcity and Sustainable Agriculture in Semiarid Environment |pages=87–109 |editor-last=García Tejero |editor-first=Iván Francisco |access-date=2023-05-21 |publisher=Academic Press |language=en |isbn=978-0-12-813164-0 |last2=Corell |first2=Mireia |last3=Galindo |first3=Alejandro |last4=Pérez-López |first4=David |last5=Memmi |first5=Houssem |last6=Rodríguez |first6=Pedro |last7=Cruz |first7=Zulma N. |last8=Centeno |first8=Ana |last9=Intrigliolo |first9=Diego S. |editor2-last=Durán Zuazo |editor2-first=Víctor Hugo}}</ref>

The domestication center of origin of ''P. salicina'' is southwestern China, from the Yangtze River Basin.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wei |first1=Xiao |last2=Shen |first2=Fei |last3=Zhang |first3=Qiuping |last4=Liu |first4=Ning |last5=Zhang |first5=Yuping |last6=Xu |first6=Ming |last7=Liu |first7=Shuo |last8=Zhang |first8=Yujun |last9=Ma |first9=Xiaoxue |last10=Liu |first10=Weisheng |date=2021-04-21 |title=Genetic diversity analysis of Chinese plum (Prunus salicina L.) based on whole-genome resequencing |journal=Tree Genetics & Genomes |language=en |volume=17 |issue=3 |page=26 |doi=10.1007/s11295-021-01506-x |s2cid=221399639 |issn=1614-2950|doi-access=free }}</ref> Wild populations of this species are reported as thriving in the provinces of Shaanxi and Gansu.<ref name=":5">Rhodes, L. & Maxted, N. 2016. ''Prunus salicina''. ''The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species'' 2016: e.T50247990A50247993. {{doi|10.2305/IUCN.UK.2016-3.RLTS.T50247990A50247993.en}}. Accessed on 28 January 2023.</ref> It is recorded as an introduced species in both Australia and Japan.<ref name=":4" />

== Ecology ==
''P. salicina'' is strongly dependent on [[Mycorrhiza|endomycorrhizal]] relationships, similar to other species of plums.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Role of mycorrhizae on mineral nutrition of fruit trees |url=https://www.actahort.org/books/1217/1217_34.htm |access-date=2023-01-27 |website=www.actahort.org}}</ref> [[Ectomycorrhiza]]l relationships with the fungus ''[[Hebeloma hiemale]]'' was shown to increase net growth in ''P. cerasifera  x salicina'', compared to chemical fertilizer, compost, and a control.<ref>Elbashiti, Tarek & El Kichaoui, Abboud & Ajwa, Abdallah. (2017). Evaluation the effect of ectomycorrhizal fungi on Prunus cerasifera x salicina (Rosaceae) growth compared with chemical and organic fertilizer. 6. 41-49.</ref>

The effects of the ''P. salicina'' in improving soil in karst areas in China have been mixed. A study conducted in Guiyang Karst Park, Guizhou, China, concluded that ''P. salicina'', in combination with the moss species, ''Homomallium plagiangium, Cyrto-hypnum pygmaeuman'', and ''Brachythecium perminusculum,''  and the herbs ''Veronica arvensis'' and ''Youngia japonica'', were suitable pioneer plant species to cultivate for use in restoration of regions of karstic soil erosion.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Shen |first1=J. C. |last2=Zhang |first2=Z. H. |last3=Liu |first3=R. |last4=Wang |first4=Z. H. |date=2018-12-06 |title=Ecological restoration of eroded karst utilizing pioneer moss and vascular plant species with selection based on vegetation diversity and underlying soil chemistry |journal=International Journal of Phytoremediation |volume=20 |issue=14 |pages=1369–1379 |doi=10.1080/15226514.2018.1474435 |issn=1522-6514 |pmid=30652488|s2cid=58546855 }}</ref> Planted on cropland suffering from rocky desertification, in the city of Hechi, ''P. salicina'' increased the carbon-to-nitrogen ratio and the [[soil quality]] at the 10–20 cm soil layer, though in general, it had limited influence on soil improvement because of its fast growth and high output, increasing the absorption of nutrients from the soil.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Guan |first1=Huiling |last2=Fan |first2=Jiangwen |date=2020-07-02 |title=Effects of vegetation restoration on soil quality in fragile karst ecosystems of southwest China |journal=PeerJ |language=en |volume=8 |article-number=e9456 |doi=10.7717/peerj.9456 |pmid=32676227 |pmc=7335502 |issn=2167-8359 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Cultivation==
The main producing country of Japanese plums is China, followed by the United States of America, Mexico, Italy, Spain, Pakistan, Korea, Australia, Chile, France, South Africa, and Argentina. The most famous variety of this fruit in Vietnam is the [[Tam Hoa]] plum grown in [[Bắc Hà (township)|Bắc Hà]] town, in [[Lào Cai Province]].

Japanese cultivars were introduced into the United States in the latter half of the 19th century, where subsequent breeding produced many more cultivars, generally with larger fruit. Plant breeder [[Luther Burbank]] developed a number of cultivars by hybridizing ''P. salicina'' with ''P. simonii'' and other native North American [[diploid]] plums such as ''P. americana, P. hortulana'', or ''P. munsoniana''. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries from these hybridizations, Burbank selected cultivars such as 'Beauty', 'Eldorado', 'Formosa', 'Gaviota', 'Santa Rosa', 'Shiro', and 'Wickson', some of which are still widely grown.<ref name="jones">{{cite journal|last=Jones|first=D. F.|year=1928|title=Burbank's Results with Plums|journal=Journal of Heredity|volume=19|issue=8|pages=359–372|doi=10.1093/oxfordjournals.jhered.a103021}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last1=Guerra |first1=M. E. |last2=Rodrigo |first2=J. |date=2015-12-14 |title=Japanese plum pollination: A review |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304423815302612 |journal=Scientia Horticulturae |language=en |volume=197 |pages=674–686 |doi=10.1016/j.scienta.2015.10.032 |issn=0304-4238|url-access=subscription }}</ref> One of the famous cultivars, "Santa Rosa", named after the city in California.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Boonprakob|first1=U.|last2=Byrne|first2=D.H.|date=2003|title=Species composition of Japanese plum founding clones as revealed by RAPD markers|journal=Acta Horticulturae|issue=622|pages=473–476|doi=10.17660/actahortic.2003.622.51|issn=0567-7572}}</ref>

Most of the fresh plums sold in North American supermarkets are ''P. salicina'' cultivars or hybrids. They are grown on a large scale in a number of other countries, for example, they dominate the [[Drupe|stone fruit]] industry in Western Australia.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.agric.wa.gov.au/servlet/page?_pageid=449&_dad=portal30&_schema=PORTAL30&p_start_url=/pls/portal30/docs/FOLDER/IKMP/AAP/HBH/BULLETIN4298_PLUM.HTM|title=Department of Agriculture and Food, Western Australia|date=27 September 2007|publisher=|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070927005419/http://www.agric.wa.gov.au/servlet/page?_pageid=449&_dad=portal30&_schema=PORTAL30&p_start_url=/pls/portal30/docs/FOLDER/IKMP/AAP/HBH/BULLETIN4298_PLUM.HTM|access-date=6 May 2018|archive-date=2007-09-27}}</ref> In France in 2020, Japanese plum production volumes are now higher than those of European plums.<ref>{{Cite web |title=French Ministry of Agriculture - Agreste database - 2021 data on plum production |url=https://agriculture.gouv.fr/ |access-date=2024-03-11 |website=Site internet du Ministère de l'Agriculture et de la Souveraineté alimentaire |language=fr}}</ref>

== Threats ==
In open-field cultivation, this species is vulnerable to several vector- or pollen-borne viral diseases affecting ''Prunus'' species, including [[Plum pox|plum pox virus]] and [[Prunus necrotic ringspot virus|''Prunus'' necrotic ringspot virus]]. Japanese plums are also well-known for their susceptibility to European stone-fruit yellows phytoplasma, with strong symptoms including yellowing, leaf roll, premature fruit drop, and dieback.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Marcone |first1=C. |chapter=CHAPTER 43: European Stone Fruit Yellows Phytoplasma |date=2011 |title=Virus and Virus-Like Diseases of Pome and Stone Fruits |pages=233–241 |publisher=The American Phytopathological Society |last2=Jarausch |first2=B. |last3=Jarausch |first3=W. |last4=Dosba |first4=F.|doi=10.1094/9780890545010.043 |isbn=978-0-89054-501-0 }}</ref> Additional threats to this species remain unknown, and while several known threats to the forests of China exist, including logging, deforestation, and air and water pollution, whether these have a direct effect on ''P. salicina'' is unknown. As of 2023, its threat status on the IUCN Red List is least concern, and this species' population is stable.<ref name=":5" /> The IUCN Red List recommends "the incorporation of population management and monitoring in protected areas where this species is known to occur" and  "additional ''ex situ'' collection, ensuring the full range of genetic diversity found in the wild is represented in gene banks."<ref name=":5" />

==Uses==

=== Culinary ===
Since ''P. salicina'' fruit has a short shelf-life (3–4 days) under room temperature, as well as cold storage (1–2 weeks), it is often prepared into jams, jellies, wine, and other beverages. Black pepper, coriander, cumin, clove, [[black cardamom]], saffron, nutmeg, cinnamon, poppy seed, ginger, [[Woodfordia floribunda|woodfordia]], asparagus, [[Withania somnifera|withania]], [[adhatoda]], and rosemary have been reported to be used in preparing aromatized plum wine. The 'Santa Rosa' plum cultivar produces the best-quality wine, in comparison 'Methley', and 'Green Gage'.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Panesar |first1=P. S. |chapter=Chapter 9 - Technology for Production of Fortified and Sparkling Fruit Wines |date=2017-01-01 |chapter-url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780128008508000090 |title=Science and Technology of Fruit Wine Production |pages=487–530 |editor-last=Kosseva |editor-first=Maria R. |place=San Diego |publisher=Academic Press |language=en |isbn=978-0-12-800850-8 |access-date=2023-01-28 |last2=Joshi |first2=V. K. |last3=Bali |first3=V. |last4=Panesar |first4=R. |editor2-last=Joshi |editor2-first=V. K. |editor3-last=Panesar |editor3-first=P. S.}}</ref>

In China, candied fruits are also sold preserved, flavoured with sugar, salt, and [[liquorice]]. A study on foraging in the Gongba Valley (Zhouqu County in Gansu, China) identified ''P. salicina'' as one of the most commonly eaten wild fruits.<ref name=":5" /> Liquor made from ''P. salicina'' fruit is mixed with ''P. mume'' liquor, and oolong tea liquor to make a Japanese-style plum liquor, ''wumeijiu'' (smoked plum liquor), in Taiwan.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Joshi |first1=V. K. |chapter=Chapter 1 - Science and Technology of Fruit Wines: An Overview |date=2017-01-01 |chapter-url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780128008508000016 |title=Science and Technology of Fruit Wine Production |pages=1–72 |editor-last=Kosseva |editor-first=Maria R. |place=San Diego |publisher=Academic Press |language=en |isbn=978-0-12-800850-8 |access-date=2023-01-28 |last2=Panesar |first2=P. S. |last3=Rana |first3=V. S. |last4=Kaur |first4=S. |editor2-last=Joshi |editor2-first=V. K. |editor3-last=Panesar |editor3-first=P. S.}}</ref>

In Japan, while it is less commonly eaten than closely related ''P. mume'', it is pickled and colored in a similar manner. Especially in eastern Japan, many [[Ennichi|summer festivals]] sell pickled fruits covered in ''[[mizuame]]'' candy called ''anzuame'' (apricot candy, as apricots were traditionally used for the recipe).<ref>{{Cite web|last=Media|first=USEN|title=Comprehensive Guide on Japanese Food Stands in the Summer Festival|url=https://savorjapan.com/contents/discover-oishii-japan/comprehensive-guide-on-japanese-food-stands-in-the-summer-festival/|access-date=2021-06-10|website=SAVOR JAPAN|language=en}}</ref>

In both countries, it is also used half-ripe as a flavouring in a [[liqueur]] called ''sumomo shu'' (すもも酒) in Japanese.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.myttc.cn/viewpro.jsp?id=4867&proid=7033|title=桃形李酒系列·绍兴市果花香果酒有限公司|date=21 October 2007|publisher=|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071021200109/http://www.myttc.cn/viewpro.jsp?id=4867&proid=7033|access-date=6 May 2018|archive-date=2007-10-21}}</ref>

== Toxicity ==
As with other stone fruits, the pit and leaves are poisonous to humans, as they contain [[amygdalin]], which breaks down to [[hydrogen cyanide]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2018-07-25 |title=Are Stone Fruit Seeds Poisonous? |url=https://www.goodhousekeeping.com/health/diet-nutrition/a20705824/are-stone-fruit-seeds-poisonous/ |access-date=2023-01-28 |website=Good Housekeeping |language=en-us}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Poisonous and Non-poisonous Plants |url=https://www.poison.org/articles/plant |access-date=2023-01-28 |website=www.poison.org |language=en}}</ref> While poisoning from unintentional ingestion of a few pits is unlikely, avoiding ingestion, especially of crushed pits, is recommended.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Swallowing fruit seeds |url=https://www.poison.org/tips/fruit-seeds |access-date=2023-01-28 |website=www.poison.org |language=en}}</ref>
